title: How Indian Entrepreneur Deepankar Rustagi Turned $50,000 Into a $120 Million Platform Digitizing Africa's Retail Economy
excerpt: Rustagi's Omnibiz connects millions of small African retailers to manufacturers through digital supply chain tools, processing over $849 million in transactions.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Deepankar Rustagi transformed $50,000 into a $120 million platform for African retailers.
  • OmniRetail partners with over 200 brands and 70 logistics providers in Nigeria and Ghana.
  • The platform processed $849 million in sales transactions last year.
  • Rustagi identified a gap in Africa's informal trade and digital infrastructure.
  • OmniRetail aims to expand its digital services across West Africa.

  • Indian entrepreneur Deepankar Rustagi built Omnibiz (now OmniRetail) from an initial $50,000 investment into a $120 million platform connecting African small retailers to the digital economy
  • The platform partners with over 200 brands and 70+ logistics partners across Nigeria and Ghana, processing 1.3 trillion naira ($849 million) in sales transactions
  • Omnibiz raised $29 million in funding and operates an asset-light model offering data-driven inventory, warehousing, logistics and financial solutions
  • Rustagi has lived in Nigeria for over two decades, identifying the gap between Africa's massive informal trade economy and digital infrastructure

More than a decade after leaving India for Africa, Deepankar Rustagi has built one of the continent's most consequential retail technology platforms. What started with $50,000 and roughly $300,000 from family and friends has grown into OmniRetail (formerly Omnibiz), a $120 million supply chain platform that connects millions of small African retailers to the formal digital economy.

The company, backed by $29 million in venture funding, partners with over 200 consumer brands and 70-plus logistics providers across Nigeria and Ghana. It processed 1.3 trillion naira — approximately $849 million — in sales transactions last year alone, according to Rustagi.

Spotting What Others Missed

Rustagi's insight was deceptively simple. Africa's informal retail sector accounts for roughly 90 percent of consumer sales in major economies, according to PwC research. Yet these millions of one-person stalls and small shops operated with virtually no digital visibility or structured data.

"You had millions of small businesses operating daily, employing huge numbers of people, but there was almost no structured digital data around them. These businesses were effectively invisible to the online world."

— Deepankar Rustagi, Founder and CEO, OmniRetail

Rustagi first arrived in Nigeria and launched VConnect in 2011, an online marketplace that connected individuals with local service professionals. After that venture wound down in 2017, he spent time consulting for major FMCG brands and identified the core inefficiency: manufacturers had no efficient way to reach the millions of small retailers who actually sold their products to consumers.

How the Platform Works

OmniRetail operates an asset-light model. Retailers can place orders through a mobile app, WhatsApp channel or phone number, sourcing products directly from manufacturers at their convenience. The platform handles the digital supply chain — inventory management, warehousing, logistics coordination and financial solutions — without owning delivery assets itself.

Major manufacturers including Flour Mills of Nigeria, Guinness and Coca-Cola use the platform. Guinness has cut distribution costs by as much as 20 percent through OmniRetail, according to CEO Girish Sharma. Flour Mills has used the platform's real-time market demand data to expand into Ghana and Francophone West Africa.

A Diaspora Success Story

Rustagi's trajectory mirrors a broader pattern of Indian entrepreneurs finding opportunity in emerging markets outside the traditional Silicon Valley track. His story highlights the Indian diaspora's global commercial footprint — Indians have long played significant roles in African economies, particularly in East Africa, and Rustagi's venture represents a modern, technology-driven iteration of that historical connection.

The company's success also demonstrates that India-born founders are building consequential businesses well beyond the US tech corridor that dominates diaspora achievement narratives.

What's Next

OmniRetail raised a combined $31 million this year alongside partner Koolboks to expand operations. The company is positioning itself to become the default digital infrastructure for informal retail across West Africa, with plans to expand beyond Nigeria and Ghana. For the millions of small retailers it serves, the platform's promise is straightforward: better access to goods means more income and more stability in economies where informal commerce is not a fringe activity but the dominant form of trade.
